items.model: The policy is weak. Six letters is far too short: a computer can try every combination quickly in a brute-force attack, and letters only gives fewer possibilities than mixing letters, digits and symbols. Weekly changes sound secure but make people choose simple, predictable passwords, and allowing sticky notes means anyone walking past can read them. A better policy would require long passphrases (for example three random words and a number), no forced weekly changes, a lock-out after several wrong attempts, and two-factor authentication, while never writing the password down where others can see it.

items.example: A like button that changes the moment you tap it is run by JavaScript.

items.hook: **COUNT counts rows, SUM adds, AVG averages, ORDER BY sorts.**
items.example: A music app’s “most played” list is a query sorted with ORDER BY plays DESC.

items.prompt: Why is “name” a poor choice of primary key for a table of students?

options.text: Two students might share a name, but keys must be unique
Names are too short to work as a primary key
options.feedback: The problem is that names can repeat.

options.text: Names cannot be stored in a key field, only numbers
options.feedback: They can; they just are not unique.

items.explain: Schools use a student ID number as the primary key instead.
items.hook: **Primary key = unique**, so names are out and ID numbers are in.
items.example: A library card number is a primary key: it picks out exactly one member.

items.prompt: What does SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Heroes; return?

options.text: The number of records in the table
Every field of every record in the table
options.feedback: That is SELECT *.

options.text: The largest value
options.feedback: That would be MAX.

items.explain: COUNT, SUM, MAX, MIN and AVG are aggregate functions: they summarise many rows into one answer.
items.hook: **COUNT counts rows**; SUM adds, MAX finds the biggest.
items.example: A shop asking “how many orders came in today?” runs a COUNT query.

items.prompt: Which query lists heroes from strongest to weakest?

options.text: SELECT name FROM Heroes ORDER BY strength DESC;
SELECT name FROM Heroes ORDER BY strength ASC;
options.feedback: ASC is weakest first.

options.text: SELECT name FROM Heroes WHERE strength;
options.feedback: WHERE filters rows; it does not sort.

items.explain: DESC = descending, biggest first.
items.hook: **DESC = descending = biggest first; ASC = ascending = smallest first.**
items.example: Sorting a shop by “price: high to low” is ORDER BY price DESC.

items.prompt: Why do big organisations use databases rather than spreadsheets?

options.text: Many users can share huge amounts of data safely
Spreadsheets are too expensive for big organisations
options.feedback: Cost is not the main reason; scale and safe sharing are.

options.text: Spreadsheets cannot store numbers with decimals
options.feedback: They can, but they struggle with millions of records and many users.

items.explain: Databases enforce data types, keys and permissions, and answer queries very fast.
items.hook: **Databases: many users, millions of records, all kept safe.**
items.example: Airlines use databases so that two people can never book the same seat at the same moment.

items.prompt: In SQL, which wildcard in LIKE means “any number of characters”?
items.explain: LIKE 'A%' matches anything starting with A.
items.hook: **% means any number of characters** in LIKE, so A% means “starts with A”.

items.prompt: A museum keeps a database of Greek vases. Explain why each vase record needs a primary key, and suggest a good field to use.
hints: Say what a primary key is (unique for every record)
Explain a problem without one (duplicates, finding or updating the wrong record)
Suggest a suitable field and say why other fields would not work
items.model: A primary key is a field whose value is different for every record, so each vase can be identified exactly. Without one, two vases with the same description, painter or date would be impossible to tell apart, and updating or deleting “the red-figure amphora” might change the wrong record. A good primary key is a catalogue number such as VASE-0451, given to each vase when it arrives. Fields like painter or date are poor choices because many vases share them.

items.prompt: How does a machine-learning system learn to recognise owls in photos?

options.text: It is trained on many labelled photos of owls
A programmer writes a rule for every possible owl
options.feedback: That is impossible; it learns from examples.

options.text: It looks up the answer on the internet each time
options.feedback: It uses the patterns it learned in training.

items.explain: Machine learning finds patterns in training data rather than following hand-written rules.
items.hook: **Machine learning = learning from examples**, not from hand-written rules.
items.example: Email spam filters learn from millions of messages that people have marked as spam.

items.prompt: A face-recognition system was trained mostly on photos of one group of people. What is the likely problem?

options.text: It will be less accurate for under-represented groups
It will work perfectly for everyone, as computers are fair
options.feedback: A system is only as good as its training data.

options.text: It will only recognise faces it has seen before
options.feedback: It can recognise new faces, but less accurately for some groups.

items.explain: Biased training data leads to biased results, which can have serious real-world effects.
items.hook: **Biased data in, biased results out.**
items.example: Researchers have found some face-recognition systems were least accurate for darker-skinned women.

items.prompt: What is the Turing test?

options.text: Whether a machine’s conversation passes for a human’s
A test of how fast a computer can solve puzzles
options.feedback: It is about intelligent behaviour.

options.text: An exam that Alan Turing set for his code-breakers
options.feedback: Alan Turing proposed it in 1950 as a thought experiment.

items.explain: Turing called it the “imitation game”.
items.hook: **The Turing test is the imitation game**: can a machine pass for a human in a chat?
items.example: CAPTCHA puzzles on websites are a reverse Turing test: you prove that you are human.

items.prompt: A chatbot confidently gives a wrong date for the Battle of Marathon. What does this show?

options.text: AI can sound sure but be wrong, so check facts
Historians have recently changed the battle date
options.feedback: Marathon was in 490 BC; the chatbot was wrong.

options.text: Chatbots are never useful for history homework
options.feedback: They can be very useful, but need checking.

items.explain: Generative AI predicts likely text; it does not always know what is true.
items.hook: **AI predicts likely words, not true facts**: always check.
items.example: Lawyers have been caught quoting court cases that a chatbot simply made up.

items.prompt: The examples a machine-learning system learns from are called its…
items.explain: Good, varied, fairly collected training data is vital.
items.hook: **Training data is the textbook the AI learns from.**

items.prompt: A company wants to use AI to sort job applications. Discuss how the system could become biased and what the company should do about it.
hints: Explain that AI learns from past data
Give an example of how past decisions could be unfair
Suggest at least two ways to reduce the risk
Reach a judgement
items.model: The AI would learn from the company’s past hiring decisions. If those decisions were unfair, for example if fewer women were hired for engineering jobs, the system would learn to rate similar applicants lower and repeat the unfairness at speed, while looking objective. To reduce the risk, the company should check its training data for imbalances, test the system’s results for different groups before using it, explain how decisions are made, and keep a human reviewing the final choices. AI can save time, but only if it is checked and used responsibly.

items.hook: **1 GHz = 1 billion cycles every second.**
items.example: A 3 GHz processor ticks about 3 billion times in the second it takes you to say “one”.

items.prompt: What is cache memory?

options.text: Small, very fast memory near the CPU for frequent data
Extra hard-disk space used when RAM is full
options.feedback: Cache is much faster and much smaller than storage.

options.text: A copy of every file saved in the cloud
options.feedback: That is cloud storage, which is far slower.

items.explain: Fetching from cache is many times faster than fetching from RAM.
items.hook: **Cache = the snack drawer by your desk**: small, close and fast.

items.prompt: A quad-core CPU has four cores. Why might a program NOT run four times faster than on one core?

options.text: Some tasks must happen in order and can’t be split
Each core only runs at a quarter of the speed
options.feedback: Each core runs at full speed.

options.text: Four cores must share one clock tick between them
options.feedback: Each core runs at the clock speed.

items.explain: Software has to be written to use several cores, and some steps depend on earlier ones.
items.hook: **Some jobs can’t be shared**: four cooks can’t boil one egg four times faster.
items.example: Exporting a video keeps every core busy; loading one web page uses only one or two.

items.prompt: What is a register?

options.text: A tiny, very fast storage location in the CPU
A list of the programs that are installed
options.feedback: In a CPU it is a storage location.

options.text: A type of hard drive built into the motherboard
options.feedback: Registers are inside the CPU itself.

items.explain: The program counter register, for example, holds the address of the next instruction.
items.hook: **Registers are the CPU’s own pockets**: tiny, but the fastest storage of all.

items.prompt: In the von Neumann architecture, what is stored together in memory?

options.text: Both the program instructions and the data
Only the data, with programs in the CPU
options.feedback: The key idea is that programs are stored like data.

options.text: Only the operating system and its files
options.feedback: Instructions and data share memory.

items.explain: The stored-program idea means a computer can run any program just by loading it into memory.
items.hook: **Stored program: instructions are just data in memory.**

items.prompt: Which is an embedded system?

options.text: The computer that controls a washing machine
A laptop used for many different jobs
options.feedback: Laptops are general-purpose computers.

options.text: A web browser running on a smartphone
options.feedback: That is software, not a system inside a device.

items.explain: Embedded systems do one dedicated job inside a bigger device: cars, microwaves, traffic lights.
items.hook: **Embedded = one job, built in.**
items.example: A smart thermostat, a car’s airbag controller and a washing machine all contain embedded systems.

items.prompt: Theo says: “A computer with twice as many cores will always run my game twice as fast.” Explain whether he is right.
hints: Explain what a core is
Explain why some tasks cannot be shared between cores
Mention at least one other factor (clock speed, cache, the graphics card, RAM)
Reach a judgement
items.model: Theo is not right. Each core can run instructions at the same time as the others, so more cores help when work can be split into independent parts. But many parts of a game depend on each other and must happen in order, and the game has to be written to use several cores at all, so the extra cores may sit idle. Speed also depends on clock speed, the size of the cache, the amount of RAM and, for games, especially the graphics card. Twice the cores may help, but it will rarely double the speed.

items.prompt: Which is NOT a job of the operating system?

options.text: Writing your history essay for you
Managing memory
options.feedback: The OS shares memory between programs.

options.text: Controlling devices through drivers
options.feedback: That is an OS job.

items.explain: The OS manages memory, the processor, devices, files, users and security, and provides the user interface.
items.hook: **The OS is the manager, not the worker**: it won’t write your essay.

items.prompt: How can a single-core computer seem to run music, a browser and a game at the same time?

options.text: The OS switches between them very fast
Each program secretly gets its own hidden CPU
options.feedback: There is only one core.

options.text: The programs take turns, each for an hour
options.feedback: Switching happens thousands of times a second.

items.explain: This is called multitasking, and scheduling the processor is a key OS job.
items.hook: **Multitasking is super-fast juggling**: the CPU switches between tasks.
items.example: Music keeps playing while you browse because the OS switches the processor between them many times a second.

items.prompt: What does a device driver do?

options.text: Lets the OS communicate with a piece of hardware
Installs new hardware inside the computer case
options.feedback: It is software!

options.text: Speeds up the internet by compressing data
options.feedback: It is about controlling hardware.

items.explain: Each printer, graphics card or controller needs a driver so the OS knows how to talk to it.
items.hook: **A driver is a translator** between the OS and one piece of hardware.
items.example: Plugging in a new printer or games controller often installs a driver first.

items.prompt: Why should you not defragment a solid-state drive (SSD)?

options.text: It doesn’t speed an SSD up and adds wear
SSDs cannot store files in fragments at all
options.feedback: They store files very well.

options.text: Defragmenting deletes the files stored on an SSD
options.feedback: It rearranges them; on an SSD there is no benefit.

items.explain: Defragmenting helps spinning hard disks, where scattered pieces of a file slow reading down.
items.hook: **Defragmenting helps spinning disks, not SSDs**: an SSD has no moving head to wait for.

items.prompt: What is open-source software?

options.text: Software whose source code anyone can read and change
Software that stays open on screen in the background
options.feedback: It is about the source code.

options.text: Software that has been tested to have no bugs
options.feedback: Open-source software has bugs like any other.

items.explain: Linux and Firefox are open source; Windows is proprietary (closed source).
items.hook: **Open source = an open recipe**: anyone can read and change it.
items.example: Android is built on the open-source Linux kernel.

items.prompt: Which utility copies files to another place so they can be recovered if lost?
items.explain: A good habit is the 3-2-1 rule: three copies, on two kinds of storage, one kept somewhere else.
items.hook: **3-2-1: three copies, two kinds of storage, one kept somewhere else.**
items.example: A phone that backs up its photos to the cloud each night is keeping a copy somewhere else.

items.prompt: Under the Data Protection Act (UK GDPR), which is a principle organisations must follow?

options.text: Personal data must be kept no longer than necessary
Personal data may be sold to anyone
options.feedback: That would break the law.

options.text: People have no right to see the data held about them
options.feedback: People have the right to access their data.

items.explain: Data must be used fairly and lawfully, for stated purposes, kept accurate and secure, and not kept longer than needed.
items.hook: **Keep only what you need, only for as long as you need it.**
items.example: A shop shouldn’t keep your card details for years after a single online order.

items.prompt: Kit guesses his friend’s password and logs into her account “just to look”. Which law has he broken?

options.text: The Computer Misuse Act 1990
The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act
options.feedback: That is about copying creative work.

options.text: No law, because he only looked
options.feedback: Unauthorised access is an offence even if nothing is changed.

items.explain: Unauthorised access is the first offence under the Computer Misuse Act; doing it to commit further crimes, or to damage data, are more serious offences.
items.hook: **Unauthorised access is a crime**, even “just to look”.
items.example: Guessing a teacher’s password to peek at test answers would break the Computer Misuse Act.

items.prompt: Mira uploads a whole film she did not make to her own website. Which law covers this?

options.text: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
The Data Protection Act 2018 (UK GDPR)
options.feedback: That is about personal data.

options.text: The Computer Misuse Act 1990
options.feedback: That is about hacking.

items.explain: Copyright protects films, music, books and software from being copied and shared without permission.
items.hook: **CDPA 1988 = Copyright, Designs and Patents**: don’t copy and share other people’s work.
items.example: Video sites take down uploaded films and songs after copyright complaints.

items.prompt: Why is e-waste (old phones and laptops) an environmental problem?

options.text: Toxic materials and valuable metals are dumped, not recycled
Phones release harmful radio waves when thrown away
options.feedback: They contain metals, plastics and chemicals.

options.text: E-waste is always recycled perfectly in the UK
options.feedback: Much of it is not.

items.explain: Recycling recovers metals like gold and copper and stops toxic chemicals leaking into soil and water.
items.hook: **E-waste: poison inside, and treasure inside.**
items.example: The UK throws away more electronic waste per person than almost any other country.

items.prompt: Why do data centres affect the environment?

options.text: They use huge amounts of electricity for power and cooling
They are all built underwater to keep them cool
options.feedback: Almost all are on land.

options.text: They have no effect, as they run on solar power
options.feedback: Their electricity and water use is significant.

items.explain: Streaming, cloud storage and AI all run in data centres, so their energy use is growing fast.
items.hook: “**The cloud is just someone else’s computer**”, and it needs power and cooling.
items.example: Some data centres are built in cold places such as Iceland and Scandinavia to save on cooling.

items.prompt: What is the digital divide?

options.text: The gap between people with and without good internet access
The split between people who use Apple and Android
options.feedback: It is a social idea.

options.text: Dividing a file into packets to send online
options.feedback: That is packet switching.

items.explain: Cost, location, age and skills can all leave people behind as more services move online.
items.hook: **The divide is the gap between online and offline.**
items.example: Older people without the internet can struggle as banks close branches and move services online.

items.hook: **Base case + a smaller call**: factorial(n) = n × factorial(n − 1), stopping at 1.
items.example: Russian dolls: open each doll to find a smaller one, until the tiny solid doll, the base case.

items.prompt: What happens if a recursive function has no base case?

options.text: It calls itself until it runs out of memory
It returns 0 because nothing was calculated
options.feedback: Without a base case nothing stops the calls.

options.text: It runs once and then stops by itself
options.feedback: It never stops calling itself.

items.explain: Python stops it with a RecursionError when the call stack gets too deep.
items.hook: **No base case = no brakes.**
items.example: Two mirrors facing each other make an endless corridor of reflections: recursion with no base case.

items.prompt: Any recursive function could also be written with…

options.text: a loop (iteration)
only a dictionary
options.feedback: A loop can do the same job.

options.text: nothing else
options.feedback: Recursion and iteration are interchangeable, though one is often clearer.

items.explain: Recursion is elegant for problems that contain smaller copies of themselves, like trees and mazes.
items.hook: **Recursion and loops are two roads to the same place.**

items.prompt: A function that calls itself is called…
items.explain: Each call works on a smaller version of the problem.
items.hook: **Recursive = it calls itself**, each time on a smaller problem.
items.example: Searching a folder that has folders inside folders is naturally done recursively.

items.hook: **BFS: ripples on a pond. Dijkstra: always extend the shortest route found so far.**
items.example: Sat navs and delivery firms use shortest-path algorithms to plan their routes.

items.prompt: In a graph of islands and sea routes, what are the islands called?

options.text: Nodes (or vertices)
Edges (or arcs)
options.feedback: The routes are the edges.

options.text: Weights (or costs)
options.feedback: Weights are the distances on the edges.

items.explain: Graphs model maps, networks, friendships and much more.
items.hook: **Nodes are the dots; edges are the lines between them.**
items.example: A social network is a graph: people are the nodes and friendships are the edges.

items.prompt: Why does breadth-first search find the route with the fewest steps?

options.text: It checks all squares 1 step away, then 2, and so on
It always turns left at every junction it meets
options.feedback: That is a maze-walking trick, not BFS.

options.text: It picks the direction closest to the exit
options.feedback: BFS is systematic.

items.explain: The first time BFS reaches the exit, no shorter route can exist.
items.hook: **BFS = ripples spreading out**: everything 1 step away, then 2, then 3.
items.example: Social apps can find “friends of friends” with a breadth-first search.

items.prompt: Which everyday technology uses shortest-path algorithms like Dijkstra’s?

options.text: Sat navs and map apps
Calculators
options.feedback: Calculators do arithmetic, not routes.

options.text: Spell-checkers and grammar tools
options.feedback: They compare words, not routes.

items.explain: Internet routers use similar algorithms to choose paths for packets.
items.hook: **Dijkstra: always extend the shortest route found so far.**
items.example: Delivery firms plan van routes with shortest-path algorithms to save time and fuel.

items.hook: **Brackets first, then NOT, then AND, then OR**, and give each gate its own column in the truth table.
items.example: A seatbelt warning beeps when (the engine is on AND the seatbelt is NOT fastened).

items.prompt: How many rows does a truth table with 3 inputs need?
items.explain: 2 × 2 × 2 = 2^{3} = 8 combinations.
items.hook: **Each extra input doubles the rows**: 2³ = 8 for three inputs.

items.prompt: A half adder adds two bits. Which gates give its sum and carry outputs?

options.text: Sum: XOR; carry: AND
Sum: AND; carry: OR
options.feedback: 1 + 1 gives sum 0, carry 1: that is XOR and AND.

options.text: Sum: NOT; carry: NOT
options.feedback: NOT has only one input.

items.explain: 0+0 = 00, 0+1 = 01, 1+1 = 10: the sum bit is XOR and the carry bit is AND.

B

items.prompt: Why are NAND gates special?

options.text: Any logic circuit can be built from NANDs alone
They are the only gate with no output
options.feedback: Every gate has an output.

options.text: They only work in pairs, joined to an AND gate
options.feedback: They work alone, but combinations make every other gate.

items.explain: NAND (NOT AND) is “universal”, which is why chips can be built from huge numbers of one simple gate.
items.hook: **NAND = NOT AND, the universal gate**: you can build anything from it.
items.example: The flash memory in phones and USB sticks is called NAND flash because its memory cells are wired together in a pattern like a NAND gate.

items.hook: **Huffman: join the two least common, again and again**, to build the tree.
items.example: ZIP files and JPEG images both use Huffman coding as one of their steps.

items.prompt: Why does Huffman coding give E a short code in English text?

options.text: E is the most common letter, so it saves the most bits
E is the first letter Huffman’s algorithm reads
options.feedback: Huffman’s algorithm works from how often each letter appears, not the order it reads them.

options.text: E is a vowel, and vowels always get short codes
options.feedback: Frequency matters, not whether it is a vowel.

items.explain: Common symbols get short codes; rare symbols get long ones.
items.hook: **Common = short**, like Morse code’s single dot for E.
items.example: Morse code used the same idea: E is one dot, while the rare Q is dash, dash, dot, dash.

items.prompt: Why must no Huffman code be the start of another code?

options.text: So bits can be decoded without any separators
To make every code exactly the same length
options.feedback: Huffman codes have different lengths.

options.text: So that the file becomes lossy and smaller
options.feedback: Huffman coding is lossless.

items.explain: If A were 1 and B 10, the bits 10 could mean B or “A then something”.
items.hook: **No code is the start of another**: prefix-free, so no gaps are needed between codes.

items.prompt: Is Huffman coding lossy or lossless?
items.explain: The original text comes back exactly.
items.hook: **Huffman coding is lossless**: every letter comes back.
